danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Krigen blussede op og nærmede sig den russiske grænse. Overalt hørtes forbandelser over Bonaparte, »menneskehedens fjende«. Militsmænd og rekrutter blev indskrevet i landsbyerne, og fra krigsskuepladsen kom modstridende nyheder, falske som sædvanlig og derfor fortolket på mange måder. Livet for den gamle fyrst Bolkonskij, fyrst Andrej og fyrstinde Marja var meget forandret siden 1805.

I 1806 blev den gamle fyrst udnævnt til en af de otte øverstkommanderende, der skulle føre tilsyn med de udskrivninger, der var forordnet over hele Rusland. Trods den alderdomssvækkelse, der var blevet særlig mærkbar, siden han troede, hans søn var blevet dræbt, anså han det ikke for rigtigt at afslå en pligt, kejseren selv havde pålagt ham, og denne nye mulighed for handling gav ham fornyet energi og styrke. Han rejste uafbrudt rundt i de tre provinser, der var ham betroet, var pedantisk i opfyldelsen af sine pligter, streng til grusomhed over for sine underordnede og gik ind i alt ned til mindste detalje. Fyrstinde Marja var holdt op med at tage matematiktimer hos sin far, og når den gamle fyrst var hjemme, gik hun til hans arbejdsværelse med ammen og lille fyrst Nikolaj (som hans bedstefar kaldte ham). Barnet boede med sin amme og barnepige Savisjina i den afdøde fyrstindes værelser, og fyrstinde Marja tilbragte det meste af dagen i børneværelset, hvor hun så godt som muligt indtog en moders plads over for sin lille nevø. Mademoiselle Bourienne syntes også lidenskabeligt glad for drengen, og fyrstinde Marja berøvede sig selv for at give sin veninde fornøjelsen af at holde den lille engel — som hun kaldte sin nevø — og lege med ham.

Nær alteret i kirken på Lysye Gory fandtes et kapel over den lille fyrstindes grav, og i dette kapel stod et marmormindesmærke hentet fra Italien, forestillende en engel med udbredte vinger, klar til at flyve opad. Englens overlæbe var en smule hævet, som var den ved at smile, og en dag indrømmede fyrst Andrej og fyrstinde Marja over for hinanden, da de kom ud af kapellet, at englens ansigt underligt mindede dem om den lille fyrstinde. Men hvad der var endnu mærkeligere, skønt fyrst Andrej ikke sagde noget om det til sin søster, var, at han i det udtryk, billedhuggeren tilfældigvis havde givet englens ansigt, læste den samme milde bebrejdelse, han havde læst på sin døde kones ansigt: »Hvorfor har du gjort dette mod mig?«

Kort efter fyrst Andrejs hjemkomst overlod den gamle fyrst ham et stort gods, Bogutjarovo, omkring femogtyve kilometer fra Lysye Gory. Dels på grund af de trykkende erindringer forbundet med Lysye Gory, dels fordi fyrst Andrej ikke altid følte sig i stand til at bære sin fars egenrådighed, og dels fordi han havde brug for ensomhed, benyttede fyrst Andrej sig af Bogutjarovo, begyndte at bygge og tilbragte det meste af sin tid dér.

Efter Austerlitz-felttoget havde fyrst Andrej fast besluttet ikke at fortsætte sin militære tjeneste, og da krigen begyndte igen og alle måtte gøre tjeneste, tog han en post under sin far i udskrivningen for at undgå aktiv tjeneste. Den gamle fyrst og sønnen syntes at have byttet roller siden felttoget i 1805. Den gamle mand, oplivet af aktivitet, forventede de bedste resultater af det nye felttog, mens fyrst Andrej tværtimod, der ikke deltog i krigen og i hemmelighed fortrød det, kun så den mørke side.

Den 26. februar 1807 tog den gamle fyrst ud på en af sine inspektionsrejser. Fyrst Andrej blev som sædvanlig på Lysye Gory under faderens fravær. Lille Nikolaj havde været syg i fire dage. Kusken, der havde kørt den gamle fyrst til byen, kom tilbage med papirer og breve til fyrst Andrej.
Da tjeneren ikke fandt den unge fyrst i hans arbejdsværelse, gik han med brevene til fyrstinde Marjas gemakker, men fandt ham heller ikke dér. Man sagde ham, at fyrsten var gået op i børneværelset.

»Om jeg må bede, Deres Excellence, Petrusja har bragt nogle papirer,« sagde en af barnepigerne til fyrst Andrej, der sad på en lille barnestol og med rynket pande og skælvende hænder dryppede dråber fra en medicinflask ned i et vandglas.
»Hvad er det?« sagde han gnaven, og idet hans hånd uvilkårligt rystede, hældte han for mange dråber i glasset. Han kastede blandingen på gulvet og bad om mere vand. Pigen bragte det.

I rummet stod en barneseng, to kasser, to lænestole, et bord, et barnebord og den lille stol, som fyrst Andrej sad på. Gardinerne var trukket for, og et eneste stearinlys brændte på bordet, afskærmet af et indbundet nodehæfte, så lyset ikke faldt på barnesengen.
»Min kære,« sagde fyrstinde Marja henvendt til sin bror fra sin plads ved barnesengen, »lad os hellere vente lidt ... senere ...«
»Åh, hold dog op, du taler altid vrøvl og udsætter ting — og det er det, der kommer ud af det!« sagde fyrst Andrej i et opbragt hvisk, tydeligt med den hensigt at såre sin søster.
»Min kære, virkelig ... det er bedre ikke at vække ham ... han sover,« sagde fyrstinden i en bønlig tone.
Fyrst Andrej rejste sig og gik på tåspidser hen til barnesengen med glasset i hånden.
»Vi bør måske virkelig lade være med at vække ham,« sagde han tøvende.

»Som du vil ... virkelig ... det tror jeg også ... men som du vil,« sagde fyrstinde Marja, tydeligvis skræmt og forvirret over, at hendes mening havde fået overtaget. Hun gjorde sin bror opmærksom på pigen, der kaldte på ham i en hvisken.

Det var den anden nat, ingen af dem havde sovet, mens de vågede over drengen, der var i høj feber. De seneste dage havde de, uden tillid til huslægen og i forventning om en anden, der var sendt bud efter til byen, forsøgt snart ét middel, snart et andet. Udmattede af søvnløshed og angst væltede de deres byrde af bekymring over på hinanden og bebrejdede og skændtes.
»Petrusja er kommet med papirer fra Deres far,« hviskede pigen.
Fyrst Andrej gik ud.
»Fanden tage dem!« mumlede han, og efter at have lyttet til de mundtlige instrukser, hans far havde sendt, og taget korrespondancen og sin fars brev, vendte han tilbage til børneværelset.
»Nå?« spurgte han.
»Stadig det samme. Vent nu for Guds skyld. Karl Ivanitj siger altid, at søvn er vigtigere end noget andet,« hviskede fyrstinde Marja med et suk.
Fyrst Andrej gik hen til barnet og følte på det. Det brændte.
»Pokker tage dig og din Karl Ivanitj!« Han tog glasset med dråberne og gik atter hen til barnesengen.
»Andrej, lad være!« sagde fyrstinde Marja.
Men han så vredt på hende, skønt også med lidelse i øjnene, og bøjede sig med glasset i hånden over barnet.
»Men jeg vil det,« sagde han. »Jeg beder dig — giv ham det!«

Fyrstinde Marja trak på skuldrene, men tog lydig glasset og kaldte på barnepigen og begyndte at give medicinen. Barnet skreg hæst. Fyrst Andrej veg sammen og greb sig til hovedet, gik ud og satte sig på en sofa i det tilstødende rum.
Han havde stadig alle brevene i hånden. Han åbnede dem mekanisk og begyndte at læse. Den gamle fyrst, af og til med forkortelser, skrev med sin store, aflange håndskrift på blåt papir som følger:

Har lige i dette øjeblik modtaget med ilbud meget glædeligt nyt — hvis det ikke er falsk. Bennigsen synes at have opnået en fuldstændig sejr over Buonaparte ved Eylau. I Petersborg jubler alle, og belønningerne til hæren er utallige. Selv om han er tysker — tillykke til ham! Jeg kan ikke finde ud af, hvad kommandanten i Kortjevo — en vis Khandrikov — foretager sig; de ekstra folk og forsyninger er stadig ikke nået frem. Galoppér straks derhen og sig, at jeg hugger hovedet af ham, hvis ikke alt er på plads inden en uge. Har modtaget endnu et brev om slaget ved Preussisch-Eylau fra Petenka — han deltog — og alt er sandt. Når inkompetente folk ikke blander sig, kan selv en tysker slå Buonaparte. Han siges at flygte i stor uorden. Se at galoppere til Kortjevo uden forsinkelse og udfør instrukserne!

Fyrst Andrej sukkede og brød seglet på endnu en konvolut. Det var et tætskrevet brev på to ark fra Bilibin. Han foldede det sammen uden at læse det og genlæste sin fars brev, der sluttede med ordene: »Galoppér til Kortjevo og udfør instrukserne!«
»Nej, undskyld, men jeg tager ikke af sted nu, før barnet har det bedre,« tænkte han og gik hen til døren og kiggede ind i børneværelset.
Fyrstinde Marja stod stadig ved barnesengen og vuggede barnet forsigtigt.

»Nåja, og hvad mere ubehageligt sagde han?« tænkte fyrst Andrej, idet han mindedes sin fars brev. »Ja, vi har vundet en sejr over Bonaparte, netop nu, hvor jeg ikke gør tjeneste. Ja, ja, han gør altid nar af mig ... Nå ja, lad ham!« Og han begyndte at læse Bilibins brev, der var skrevet på fransk. Han læste uden at forstå halvdelen, læste kun for at glemme, om så blot for et øjeblik, hvad han alt for længe og alt for smertefuldt havde tænkt på med udelukkelse af alt andet.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The war was blazing and drawing nearer to the Russian frontier. Everywhere one heard curses against Bonaparte, "the enemy of mankind." Militia members and recruits were being enrolled in the villages, and from the front came contradictory news — false as usual, and therefore interpreted in every possible way. The life of old Prince Bolkonski, Prince Andrew, and Princess Mary had changed greatly since 1805.

In 1806 the old prince was made one of eight commanders in chief appointed to oversee the recruitment decreed throughout Russia. Despite the weakness of age — which had become especially noticeable since the time he thought his son had been killed — he did not feel right about refusing a duty the Emperor himself had assigned him, and this fresh opportunity for action gave him new energy and strength. He was constantly traveling through the three provinces entrusted to him, was meticulous to the point of tyranny with his subordinates, and personally looked into every detail. Princess Mary had stopped taking mathematics lessons from her father, and when the old prince was home she would go to his study with the wet nurse and little Prince Nicholas (as his grandfather called him). Baby Nicholas lived with his wet nurse and nanny Savishna in the late princess's rooms, and Princess Mary spent most of the day in the nursery, doing her best to take a mother's place with her little nephew. Mademoiselle Bourienne, too, seemed passionately fond of the boy, and Princess Mary often gave up her own time so her friend could have the pleasure of cuddling the little angel — as she called her nephew — and playing with him.

Near the altar of the church at Bald Hills there was a chapel over the tomb of the little princess, with a marble monument brought from Italy representing an angel with outspread wings ready to fly upward. The angel's upper lip was slightly raised as though about to smile, and once, on coming out of the chapel, Prince Andrew and Princess Mary admitted to each other that the angel's face reminded them uncannily of the little princess. But what was stranger still — though Prince Andrew said nothing about it to his sister — was that in the expression the sculptor had happened to give the angel's face, he read the same gentle reproach he had seen on the face of his dead wife: "Oh, why have you done this to me?"

Soon after Prince Andrew's return, the old prince gave him a large estate, Bogucharovo, about twenty-five miles from Bald Hills. Partly because of the painful memories associated with Bald Hills, partly because Prince Andrew didn't always feel up to bearing his father's eccentricities, and partly because he needed solitude, he began building at Bogucharovo and spent most of his time there.

After the Austerlitz campaign, Prince Andrew had firmly resolved not to continue his military service, and when the war resumed and everyone had to serve, he took a position under his father in the recruitment office so as to avoid active duty. The old man and his son seemed to have swapped roles since the 1805 campaign. The old prince, energized by activity, expected the best from the new campaign, while Prince Andrew, taking no part in the war and secretly regretting it, saw only the dark side.

On February 26, 1807, the old prince set off on one of his tours of inspection. Prince Andrew remained at Bald Hills as usual during his father's absence. Little Nicholas had been unwell for four days. The coachman who had driven the old prince to town returned with papers and letters for Prince Andrew.
Not finding the young prince in his study, the valet took the letters to Princess Mary's rooms, but didn't find him there either. He was told that the prince had gone to the nursery.

"If you please, your excellency, Petrusha has brought some papers," said one of the nursemaids to Prince Andrew, who was sitting on a child's little chair, frowning and with trembling hands, pouring drops from a medicine bottle into a glass half full of water.
"What is it?" he said irritably, and his hand shaking involuntarily, he poured too many drops into the glass. He threw the mixture on the floor and asked for more water. The maid brought it.

In the room were a child's crib, two trunks, two armchairs, a table, a child's table, and the little chair on which Prince Andrew sat. The curtains were drawn, and a single candle burned on the table, shielded by a bound music book so the light wouldn't fall on the crib.
"My dear," said Princess Mary, addressing her brother from beside the crib where she was standing, "better wait a bit... later..."
"Oh, stop it — you always talk nonsense and put things off — and this is what comes of it!" said Prince Andrew in an exasperated whisper, clearly intending to wound his sister.
"My dear, really... it's better not to wake him... he's asleep," the princess said pleadingly.
Prince Andrew got up and went on tiptoe to the little bed, glass in hand.
"Maybe we really shouldn't wake him," he said, hesitating.

"As you wish... really... I think so... but as you wish," said Princess Mary, clearly intimidated and flustered that her opinion had prevailed. She drew her brother's attention to the maid who was calling him in a whisper.

It was the second night that neither of them had slept, watching over the boy who was running a high fever. For days now, distrusting their household doctor and waiting for another they had sent for from town, they had been trying one remedy after another. Worn out by sleeplessness and anxiety, they took out their distress on each other, bickering and blaming.
"Petrusha has come with papers from your father," the maid whispered.
Prince Andrew went out.
"Damn it all!" he muttered, and after listening to the verbal instructions his father had sent and collecting the correspondence and his father's letter, he returned to the nursery.
"Well?" he asked.
"Still the same. Wait, for heaven's sake. Karl Ivanich always says sleep is more important than anything," whispered Princess Mary with a sigh.
Prince Andrew went up to the child and felt him. He was burning hot.
"To hell with you and your Karl Ivanich!" He picked up the glass with the drops and went back to the crib.
"Andrew, don't!" said Princess Mary.
But he scowled at her — angrily, though with suffering in his eyes — and leaned over the infant with the glass in his hand.
"I want to," he said. "I'm asking you — give it to him!"

Princess Mary shrugged but obediently took the glass and, calling the nurse, began giving the medicine. The child screamed hoarsely. Prince Andrew winced, clutched his head, and went out to sit on a sofa in the next room.
He still had all the letters in his hand. Opening them mechanically, he began to read. The old prince, using occasional abbreviations, wrote in his large, elongated hand on blue paper:

Have just this moment received by special messenger very joyful news — if it's not false. Bennigsen seems to have won a complete victory over Buonaparte at Eylau. In Petersburg everyone is rejoicing, and the rewards sent to the army are countless. Though he is a German — I congratulate him! I can't figure out what the commander at Korchevo — a certain Khandrikov — is up to; the additional men and provisions still haven't arrived. Gallop over to him at once and tell him I'll have his head if everything isn't there within a week. Also received another letter about the Preussisch-Eylau battle from Petenka — he took part in it — and it's all true. When mischief-makers don't meddle, even a German can beat Buonaparte. He is said to be fleeing in great disorder. Mind you gallop off to Korchevo without delay and carry out instructions!

Prince Andrew sighed and broke the seal of another envelope. It was a closely written two-page letter from Bilibin. He folded it up without reading it and reread his father's letter, which ended with: "Gallop off to Korchevo and carry out instructions!"
"No, excuse me, I'm not going anywhere until the child is better," he thought, going to the door and looking into the nursery.
Princess Mary was still standing by the crib, gently rocking the baby.

"Ah yes, and what other unpleasant thing did he write?" thought Prince Andrew, recalling his father's letter. "Yes — we've won a victory over Bonaparte, just when I'm not serving. Yes, yes, he's always mocking me. Ah, well! Let him!" And he began reading Bilibin's letter, which was written in French. He read without understanding half of it — reading only to forget, if just for a moment, what he had been thinking about so painfully, to the exclusion of everything else.
